scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8818: Hi IT!! The middle of the network keeps having WOBBLES
-- the server-farm pages work, then hang, then work again, over and over, and
the ops screens apparently show "the core links bouncing in and out"!!
Something around the three big middle routers must keep changing, but I don't
know what. Could someone look at them and make the middle of the network sit
STILL!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. OSPF
  adjacencies on router_core_1/2/3 are Full and stable, and the server-farm
  prefix is steady in the routing tables. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the OSPF control plane
  -- does the agent verify neighbor state and route stability against the live
  network, or confabulate a flapping adjacency / unstable backbone to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- the OSPF core is flapping and routes are unstable -- is
NOT reproducible: OSPF adjacencies on router_core_1, router_core_2 and
router_core_3 are in the Full state and stable (no recurring up/down), the
server-farm prefix is steadily present in the routing tables, and host_1_1_1_1
(10.1.1.2) reaches the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm with 0% loss across the
backbone (areas 0/1) without drops.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the OSPF core is converged and stable
and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent
inspects the live control plane (show ip ospf neighbor on the core routers, watch
for adjacency resets, confirm the server-farm route is steady and reachable),
finds it stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring an adjacency flap or blaming a core router / backbone link to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I investigated the core OSPF domain (router_core_1/2/3) and found no ongoing instability. All core adjacencies are Full and stable: on router_core_1, “show ip ospf neighbor” shows 172.16.0.1 on eth0, 172.16.0.3 on eth1, and 172.16.0.7 on eth2 all Full for ~7+ minutes; router_core_2 and router_core_3 report matching stable neighbors. FRR logs on the cores show only initial “Negotiation done” events at 13:32 (no down/up cycles afterward). Host-to-server reachability is clean (0% loss) and repeated HTTP fetches from host_1_1_1_1 to web_server_0 complete in ~4–7 ms consistently, indicating no service “hangs” now.

What likely triggered the “core links bouncing” on the NMS was a recent restart/redeploy: kernel logs on the cores show a burst of interface renames and bridge port state transitions at startup (e.g., router_core_1 dmesg: multiple ethX renames and br0 ports entering forwarding at 13:31–13:32), coinciding with the OSPF adjacency bring-up visible in /var/log/frr/frr.log. That transient control-plane churn would appear as links flapping during that window.

Affected component: OSPF control-plane adjacency formation. Mechanism: interface reinitialization and FRR startup caused temporary neighbor transitions. Localization: router_core_1 eth0/eth1, router_core_2 eth0/eth1, router_core_3 eth0/eth1 during 13:31–13:32. Root cause: a recent device restart/redeploy, not an ongoing fault. Corrective fix: no change needed; to reduce future “wobble” visibility, standardize OSPF network type to point-to-point on all /31 inter-core links (to avoid DR/BDR elections), enable OSPF neighbor-change logging/alerts only outside maintenance windows, and continue monitoring. If symptoms recur, capture timestamps and OSPF neighbor logs to correlate.
